title: UNIT 4: ELECTROMAGNETISM
notes:
✓ Electromagnetism → The study of the relationship between electricity and magnetism.

✓ Electric currents produce magnetic fields, while changing magnetic fields can produce electromotive force (emf).

◆ Applications → Motors, generators, transformers, relays, MRI machines and many electrical devices.

title: 4.1 MAGNETS AND MAGNETIC FIELD
notes:
✓ Magnet → A material that produces a magnetic field and can attract magnetic materials such as iron.

✓ Every magnet has two poles: North (N) and South (S).

✓ Like poles repel → N–N or S–S.
✓ Unlike poles attract → N–S.

✓ Magnetic poles always occur in pairs. Cutting a magnet produces smaller magnets, each with a north and south pole.

◆ PERMANENT MAGNET
✓ A permanent magnet retains its magnetic properties for a long time because its magnetism comes from the internal structure of the material.

◆ ELECTROMAGNET
✓ Electromagnet → Produces a magnetic field when electric current flows through a coil.

✓ It loses most of its magnetism when the current is switched off.
✓ An iron core can increase its magnetic strength.

◆ EARTH'S MAGNETIC FIELD
✓ Earth behaves approximately like a giant bar magnet.
✓ A compass aligns itself with Earth's magnetic field.

◆ MAGNETIC FIELD
✓ Magnetic field → The region around a magnet or moving electric charge where magnetic force acts.

✓ Magnetic field is a vector quantity.

✓ SI unit: tesla (T)

✓ Electric field → Associated with electric charges.
✓ Magnetic field → Associated with magnets and moving charges.

title: 4.2 MAGNETIC FIELD LINES
notes:
✓ Magnetic field lines → Imaginary lines used to represent the direction and strength of a magnetic field.

✓ Their density gives an indication of field strength.

◆ PROPERTIES OF MAGNETIC FIELD LINES
✓ The direction of the magnetic field is tangent to the field line.

✓ A compass points along the field direction.

✓ Closely spaced lines → Stronger magnetic field.

✓ Widely spaced lines → Weaker magnetic field.

✓ Magnetic field lines never cross.

✓ They form continuous closed loops.

✓ Outside a bar magnet → Lines go from N → S.

✓ Inside the magnet → Lines go from S → N.

◆ FIELD AROUND MAGNETS
✓ The field is strongest near the poles because the field lines are most concentrated there.

◆ MAGNETIC VS ELECTRIC FIELD LINES
✓ Electric field lines → Begin at positive charges and end at negative charges.

✓ Magnetic field lines → Have no beginning or end and form closed loops.

✓ Magnetic field lines are a visual representation; they are not physical objects.

title: 4.3 CURRENT AND MAGNETISM
notes:
✓ An electric current produces a magnetic field around a conductor.

✓ This discovery shows the close relationship between electricity and magnetism.

✓ When current flows → Magnetic field is produced.

✓ Increasing current → Stronger magnetic field.

✓ Increasing distance from the wire → Weaker magnetic field.

✓ Reversing current → Reverses the magnetic field direction.

◆ MAGNETIC FIELD AROUND A STRAIGHT WIRE
✓ The field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire are circular.

✓ B = μ₀I / 2πr

◆ Where:
B → Magnetic field strength
μ₀ → Permeability of free space
I → Current
r → Distance from the wire

✓ μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A

✓ SI unit of B: tesla (T)

◆ FLEMING'S RIGHT-HAND RULE
✓ Grip the straight wire with your right hand so that the thumb points in the direction of conventional current.

✓ The curled fingers → Show the direction of the magnetic field.

◆ APPLICATIONS
✓ The magnetic effect of current is used in electromagnets, solenoids, straight wires, cylindrical conductors and toroidal solenoids.

✓ A current-carrying coil produces a stronger and more useful magnetic field than a single straight wire, especially when an iron core is inserted.

title: 4.4 ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION
notes:
✓ Electromagnetic induction → The production of an emf when the magnetic flux through a conductor or coil changes.

✓ Michael Faraday showed that changing magnetic fields can generate electricity.

✓ Moving a magnet relative to a coil → Can induce emf.

✓ Moving the coil relative to a magnet → Can also induce emf.

✓ A changing magnetic field → Can produce an induced current if the circuit is closed.

◆ MAGNETIC FLUX (ΦB)
✓ Magnetic flux → Measures the magnetic field passing through a given area.

✓ ΦB = BA cosθ

◆ Where:
B → Magnetic field strength
A → Area of the surface
θ → Angle between B and the area vector

✓ SI unit: weber (Wb)

✓ Maximum flux occurs when θ = 0°.
✓ Zero flux occurs when θ = 90°.

✓ Greater change in magnetic flux → Greater induced emf.

✓ Faster change in flux → Greater induced emf.

✓ Basic idea:
Changing magnetic flux → Induced emf → Induced current (if the circuit is closed).

title: 4.5 FARADAY'S LAW OF ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION
notes:
✓ Faraday's law → Gives the magnitude of the emf produced by a changing magnetic flux.

◆ FARADAY'S LAW
✓ The induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux.

✓ For one turn:
ε = −ΔΦB/Δt

✓ For a coil of N turns:
ε = −NΔΦB/Δt

◆ Where:
ε → Induced electromotive force
N → Number of turns
ΔΦB → Change in magnetic flux
Δt → Change in time

◆ LENZ'S LAW
✓ The induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.

✓ The negative sign in Faraday's equation → Represents Lenz's law.

✓ Lenz's law is consistent with conservation of energy: the induced effect opposes the change rather than creating energy from nothing.

◆ TO INCREASE INDUCED EMF
✓ Increase the number of coil turns.
✓ Increase the magnetic field.
✓ Increase the coil area.
✓ Change the magnetic flux more rapidly.

◆ APPLICATION
✓ Generators → Use electromagnetic induction to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy.

title: 4.6 TRANSFORMERS
notes:
✓ Transformer → An electrical device that transfers electrical energy from one circuit to another through electromagnetic induction.

✓ It changes AC voltage without changing its frequency.

◆ MAIN PARTS
✓ Primary coil → Connected to the input AC supply.
✓ Secondary coil → Supplies the output.
✓ Iron/core → Provides a path for magnetic flux linking the coils.

◆ STEP-UP TRANSFORMER
✓ Increases output voltage.
✓ Ns > Np
✓ Vs > Vp

◆ STEP-DOWN TRANSFORMER
✓ Decreases output voltage.
✓ Ns < Np
✓ Vs < Vp

◆ TRANSFORMER EQUATION
✓ Np/Ns = Vp/Vs

◆ Where:
Np → Primary turns
Ns → Secondary turns
Vp → Primary voltage
Vs → Secondary voltage

◆ IDEAL TRANSFORMER
✓ For an ideal transformer:
VpIp = VsIs

✓ Increasing voltage → Generally corresponds to decreasing current, and vice versa.

◆ EFFICIENCY
✓ η = (Output power / Input power) × 100%

✓ Transformers operate with changing magnetic flux, so they cannot normally transform a steady DC supply.

◆ APPLICATIONS
✓ Power transmission and distribution
✓ Phone chargers
✓ Laptop chargers
✓ Microwaves
✓ X-ray equipment
✓ Many electrical systems

title: 4.7 APPLICATION AND SAFETY
notes:
✓ Electromagnetism is widely used in everyday devices and large-scale electrical systems.

◆ ELECTROMAGNETIC APPLICATIONS
✓ Electric motors → Convert electrical energy into mechanical energy.

✓ Generators → Convert mechanical energy into electrical energy.

✓ Transformers → Change AC voltage levels.

✓ Relays → Magnetically control electrical circuits.

✓ Electric bells → Use an electromagnet to produce repeated motion and sound.

✓ Headphones and loudspeakers → Use electromagnetic effects to produce sound.

✓ MRI machines → Use strong magnetic fields.

✓ Hard drives → Use magnetic effects to store information.

✓ Graphics tablets → Use changing magnetic fields to detect a pen's position.

◆ DC ELECTRIC MOTOR
✓ A current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences forces that produce torque and cause rotation.

✓ A commutator → Reverses the current appropriately so that rotation continues.

◆ AC GENERATOR
✓ An AC generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.

✓ Rotation of a coil in a magnetic field → Changes magnetic flux and produces an alternating emf according to Faraday's law.

◆ SAFETY
✓ Keep powerful electromagnets away from sensitive electronic equipment.

✓ Strong magnets can damage hard drives and affect some displays.

✓ Consider the weight of materials when using electromagnets for lifting.

✓ Air gaps between a magnet and the material being lifted → Can reduce lifting effectiveness.

✓ Electromagnetism is fundamental to modern power generation, transmission, transportation, communication and electronic technology.
